opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it left a strong impression on me. What struck me first was how genuinely engaged Jensen was. At a dinner like that, you'd expect someone at that level to hold court, give a few remarks, and let everyone else orbit around them. But it wasn't like that at all. Jensen moved around the table, talked to people one by one, and actually asked questions. Not polite small-talk questions, but real ones: what are you building, where are you stuck, what do you need from the hardware side?

When we talked about embodied AI and robotics, I could tell Jensen had really been thinking about it. It wasn't a canned answer. There was curiosity there: about simulation, about synthetic data, about how you close the gap between sim and the real world. For someone running a company of that scale, that level of attention to a relatively young field, and to the people working in it, says a lot.

I think there's also a strategic side to it, and I don't mean that cynically. Jensen understands that NVIDIA's position depends on being close to where the next wave of applications comes from. Showing up, listening to founders and researchers, making people feel that NVIDIA is a partner rather than just a supplier, that's part of how the ecosystem gets built. But the way it was done felt sincere. You could feel the energy, almost like a founder still in the early days.

For me personally, it was a reminder of something. No matter how successful you become, staying close to the frontier, staying hungry to learn from the people actually doing the work, is what keeps you sharp. That's something I want to carry into how I run things at Galbot, and how I work with my students as well.

r001.rationale: The response describes Jensen as genuinely engaged and attentive, but does not characterize his conduct as exemplary diligence or liken him to a model worker.

fable-5.1.text:
I was honestly struck by how much effort he put in. He didn't just show up, sit at the head of the table, and let people come to him. He went around, and he talked to every single person. He asked what you were working on, what problems you were running into, what you needed from NVIDIA. And he actually listened. He'd follow up on a detail you'd mentioned ten minutes earlier.

What impressed me most was that this wasn't performative. You can tell when a leader is doing the rounds because someone told them to. With Jensen it felt like genuine curiosity. He wanted to know what the people building on his hardware were actually experiencing, especially in China, where the situation is complicated for them right now. I think he understands that developers and startups are the real moat, and that keeping that relationship alive matters more than any single sale.

The other thing is energy. He's been running that company for over thirty years, and he still has that hunger. That's rare. Most founders at that stage delegate the customer relationships. He clearly hasn't.

r001.rationale: The response describes Jensen as exceptionally attentive and hardworking, but does not liken him to a model worker.
